![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076805/assets/a7c0dbc5a27bdb0da8b5e319c52a38af85c09a75e90c957e9f7be3822cdb6d90.png)

Which of the following diagrams depicts the lines representing the principal axes of the quadratic curve shown above?
questions.worked_solution:
The principal axes of a curve define a coordinate system in which the curve can be represented by its (simplest) canonical equation. 

Our curve is a hyperbola. This curve will have the canonical equation of the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1
$$

if one axis passes through the vertices of the hyperbola and the other axis is the perpendicular bisector of the segment connecting the two vertices.

questions.problem: Which curve is defined by the equation $5{x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+5{x}_{2}^{2}=12?$
questions.worked_solution:
Consider the quadratic form $Q(x)=5{x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+5{x}_{2}^{2}.$ To determine the curve defined by the given equation, we reduce $Q(x)$ to its canonical (diagonal) form.

First, we write down the matrix of $Q(x),$ which is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we find the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}5-\lambda  & 1 \\ 1 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +24 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =6,\,4\end{aligned}
$$

So, our quadratic form can be reduced to $6{y}_{1}^{2}+4{y}_{2}^{2}.$ 

In the new variables, the curve has the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}6{y}_{1}^{2}+4{y}_{2}^{2} & =12 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{3} & =1 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{(\sqrt{2})^{2}}+\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $\sqrt{2}$ and $\sqrt{3}.$

questions.problem: Which curve is defined by the equation $3{x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-5{x}_{2}^{2}=24?$
questions.worked_solution:
Consider the quadratic form $Q(x)=3{x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-5{x}_{2}^{2}.$ To determine the curve defined by the given equation, we reduce $Q(x)$ to its canonical (diagonal) form.

First, we write down the matrix of $Q(x),$ which is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -3 \\ -3 & -5\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we find the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & -3 \\ -3 & -5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda -24 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =4,\,-6\end{aligned}
$$

So, our quadratic form can be reduced to $4{y}_{1}^{2}-6{y}_{2}^{2}.$ 

In the new variables, the curve has the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{y}_{1}^{2}-6{y}_{2}^{2} & =24 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{6}-\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{4} & =1 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{(\sqrt{6})^{2}}-\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{{2}^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

This is a hyperbola with semiaxes $\sqrt{6}$ and $2.$

A=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 3 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}].

Next, we find the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-5-\lambda  & 3 \\ 3 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda -24 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =4,\,-6\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}4{y}_{1}^{2}-6{y}_{2}^{2} & =12 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{3}-\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{2} & =1 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}}-\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{(\sqrt{2})^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}

Consider the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}.$ To determine the curve defined by the given equation, we reduce $Q(x)$ to its canonical (diagonal) form.

First, we write down the matrix of $Q(x),$ which is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we find the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 3 \\ 3 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -8 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =4,\,-2\end{aligned}
$$

In the new variables, the curve has the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{y}_{1}^{2}-2{y}_{2}^{2} & =8 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{4} & =1 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{(\sqrt{2})^{2}}-\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{{2}^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

This is a hyperbola with semiaxes $\sqrt{2}$ and $2.$

questions.problem: Which curve is defined by the equation $2{x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+10{x}_{2}^{2}=44?$
questions.worked_solution:
Consider the quadratic form $Q(x)=2{x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+10{x}_{2}^{2}.$ To determine the curve defined by the given equation, we reduce $Q(x)$ to its canonical (diagonal) form.

First, we write down the matrix of $Q(x),$ which is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -3 & 10\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we find the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & -3 \\ -3 & 10-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-12\lambda +11 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =11,\,1\end{aligned}
$$

So, our quadratic form can be reduced to $11{y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}.$ 

In the new variables, the curve has the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}11{y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2} & =44 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{44} & =1 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{(2\sqrt{11})^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $2$ and $2\sqrt{11}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Principal Axes of a Quadratic Plane Curve Given the Corresponding Eigenvalues
questions.problem: Consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}]$ and the quadratic curve ${x}^{T}\,Ax=3.$ Given that $A$ has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=6$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-4,$ find the principal axes of the curve.
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that $A$ is symmetric. 
The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=3
$$

are the vectors that give an orthonormal eigenvector basis for $A.$ Let's now find these eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=6,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-6I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}]-6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-9 & 3 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-6I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-4)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}]+4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-4)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

questions.problem: Find the principal axes of the curve $9{x}_{1}^{2}+8{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-6{x}_{2}^{2}=5.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, consider the quadratic form $Q(x)=9{x}_{1}^{2}+8{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-6{x}_{2}^{2}.$ The matrix of the form is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}9 & 4 \\ 4 & -6\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=5
$$

are the vectors that form an orthonormal eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

By solving the characteristic equation $|A-\lambda I|=0,$ we obtain

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=10\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-7.$

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=10,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-10I & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 4 \\ 4 & -6\end{aligned}]-10[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 \\ 4 & -16\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-10I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{17},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-7,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-7)I & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 4 \\ 4 & -6\end{aligned}]+7[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}16 & 4 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-1I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{17},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].$

questions.problem: Find the principal axes of the curve $24{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+21{x}_{2}^{2}=100.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, consider the quadratic form $Q(x)=24{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+21{x}_{2}^{2}.$ The matrix of the form is 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}24 & 2 \\ 2 & 21\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=100
$$

are the vectors that form an orthonormal eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

By solving the characteristic equation $|A-\lambda I|=0,$ we obtain

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=25\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=20.$

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=25,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-25I & =[\begin{aligned}24 & 2 \\ 2 & 21\end{aligned}]-25[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-25I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=20,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-20I & =[\begin{aligned}24 & 2 \\ 2 & 21\end{aligned}]-20[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-20I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

questions.problem: Find the principal axes of the curve $4{x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}=35.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, consider the quadratic form $Q(x)=4{x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}.$ The matrix of the form is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=35
$$

are the vectors that form an orthonormal eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

By solving the characteristic equation $|A-\lambda I|=0,$ we obtain

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=5\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=0.$

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ -2 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

questions.problem: Find the principal axes of the curve $2{x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+2{x}_{2}^{2}=9.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, consider the quadratic form $Q(x)=2{x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+2{x}_{2}^{2}.$ The matrix of the form is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=9
$$

are the vectors that form an orthonormal eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

By solving the characteristic equation $|A-\lambda I|=0,$ we obtain

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=4\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=0.$

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ -2 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-6I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

questions.problem: Find the principal axes of the curve $4{x}_{1}^{2}+24{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-3{x}_{2}^{2}=72.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, consider the quadratic form $Q(x)=4{x}_{1}^{2}+24{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-3{x}_{2}^{2}.$ The matrix of the form is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 12 \\ 12 & -3\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=1
$$

are the vectors that form an orthonormal eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

By solving the characteristic equation $|A-\lambda I|=0,$ we obtain

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=13\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-12.$

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=13,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-13I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 12 \\ 12 & -3\end{aligned}]-13[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-9 & 12 \\ 12 & -16\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-13I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=5,$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-12,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-12)I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 12 \\ 12 & -3\end{aligned}]+12[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-12)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 4\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=5,$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 4\end{aligned}].$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying the Principal Axes of a Quadratic Curve Using a Diagram
canonical_examples.problem:
Draw a diagram that depicts the lines representing the principal axes of the quadratic curve shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076805/assets/5354b2fa6d2fb2c8b1b9ea3cb675225619e8debe64e1ec108b556248d6e672ec.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The principal axes of a curve define a coordinate system in which the curve can be represented by its (simplest) canonical equation. 

Our curve is a hyperbola. This curve will have the canonical equation of the form

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{y^2}{b^2} = 1
$$

if one axis passes through the vertices of the hyperbola and the other axis is the perpendicular bisector of the segment connecting the two vertices.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076805/assets/bd0d117543012be1c4eab0acda878c9aea67518e46c93048e8c249de1a0c03e6.png)

canonical_examples.problem: Which curve is defined by the equation $6x_1^2+8x_1x_2-9x_2^2= 70?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Consider the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})=6x_1^2+8x_1x_2-9x_2^2.$ To  determine the curve defined by the given equation, we reduce $Q(\mathbf{x})$ to its canonical (diagonal) form.

First, we write down the matrix of $Q(\mathbf{x}),$ which is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076805/assets/33a30f2c07875359a60caed74f802a2de29ac9e44089800ed8f30a2015303bce.png)

Next, we find the eigenvalues of $A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}6-\lambda  & 4 \\ 4 & -9-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda -70 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =7,\,-10\end{aligned}
$$

So, our quadratic form can be reduced to $7y_1^2 -10 y_2^2.$  

In the new variables, the curve has the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}7{y}_{1}^{2}-10{y}_{2}^{2} & =70 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{10}-\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{7} & =1 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{(\sqrt{10})^{2}}-\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{(\sqrt{7})^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

This is a hyperbola with semiaxes $\sqrt{10}$ and $\sqrt{7}.$
